authoredPrompt: This figure sets a three-dimensional rendering of a lipid bilayer beside the flat structural formula of the molecule that builds it. On the left, a slab of membrane is drawn in perspective with a stepped cutaway at one corner: rows of small green spheres tile the top and bottom faces, and the interior between them is packed with pale tan wavy strands that meet tip to tip along the slab's midplane, so the two leaflets face each other tails inward. On the right, a glycerophospholipid is drawn with a vertical glycerol backbone reading CH2, CH, CH2 from top to bottom. The topmost branch is printed in green and reads CH2-O-P(=O)(O-)-O-CH2CH2N(CH3)3+, tagged by a green arrow labeled "Ionic head". The two lower branches each run through O-C(=O) into a long tan ribbon of the same shade and waviness as the strands filling the slab, and a magenta label "Nonpolar tails" sends two arrows to their free ends. Matching the green and tan across the two halves lets the reader place each region of the drawn molecule at its position in the assembled sheet. The pairing accounts for how a long nonpolar tail bound to a polar ionic head drives aggregation into a bilayer that keeps hydrocarbon away from water.
authoredInteractions:
- Click ionic head, glycerol linker, or nonpolar tails: the selected part highlights in the molecule and in the bilayer slab, mapping amphiphilic structure to membrane organization.
- Toggle between molecule and assembly mapping: switch named highlights for ionic head, glycerol linker, and nonpolar tails, and matching regions glow on both the structural formula and membrane slab, showing how each part of one glycerophospholipid maps into the bilayer.
- Slider for cutaway depth: move the slice plane through the slab, and successive layers expose heads, tails, and the midplane tail contact, making the outside-polar/inside-nonpolar organization visible through the membrane thickness.
authoredContext:
Phospholipids are found widely in both plant and animal tissues and make up approximately 50% to 60% of cell membranes. Because they are like soaps in having a long, nonpolar hydrocarbon tail bound to a polar ionic head, phospholipids in the cell membrane organize into a lipid bilayer about 5.0 nm (50 Å) thick. As shown in the figure, the nonpolar tails aggregate in the center of the bilayer in much the same way that soap tails aggregate in the center of a micelle. This bilayer serves as an effective barrier to the passage of water, ions, and other components into and out of cells.

Aggregation of glycerophospholipids into the lipid bilayer that composes cell membranes.

Glycerophospholipids combine with the lipid bilayer comprising a cell membrane. An arrow points to the ionic head and two nonpolar tails of the lipid bilayer.

discrepancies: The molecular diagram is rendered as a 3D ball-and-stick model rather than the flat 2D structural formula (CH2/CH labels, P=O double bonds, N(CH3)3 notation) of the source; chemical-formula text is absent

The source molecule's head is drawn as plain lines/text with only the annotation 'Ionic head' in green, while the generated molecule colors the whole head group green — acceptable mapping choice but visually busier than the source
Source tails are two straight, nearly parallel wavy lines; generated tails diverge and wander in 3D depth

Slab in the source is shown only as a corner cut with one visible head layer edge-on; generated slab is a full box with heads tiling both entire faces (compositionally fine, but denser/more block-like than the source sketch)
evaluation.notes: Strong teaching artifact: faithful bilayer slab with heads-out/tails-in organization, correct color scheme, meaningful highlight-mapping buttons and a working cutaway slider; main loss is replacing the 2D structural formula with a ball-and-stick model, dropping the chemical notation detail.
action_items: Add atom/bond text annotations (CH2, CH, O, P, N(CH3)3, +/− charges) near the molecule so it reads as the structural formula in the source, not just a generic ball-and-stick model
Make the two molecule tails run straight and parallel like the source's wavy horizontal lines rather than diverging
Reduce slab depth/density slightly or angle the default view to echo the source's open corner-cut sketch look
